item.title: Typhoon Champi triggers presidential emergency actions across Marianas
item.description: President Donald Trump approved emergency declarations for both Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands as Super Typhoon Champi approached the Marianas over the weekend, authorizing federal assistance to support life‑safety and protective measures across the region. The White House granted Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero’s request for a Presidential Emergency Declaration ahead of Champi’s
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump approved emergency declarations for both Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands as Super Typhoon Champi approached the Marianas over the weekend, authorizing federal assistance to support life‑safety and protective measures across the region.

The White House granted Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero’s request for a Presidential Emergency Declaration ahead of Champi’s closest approach to Guam early Sunday morning.

“We are grateful for the president’s quick response,” Leon Guerrero said. “Along with our federal partners, we will continue seeing to the needs and protection and safety of our people.”

Lt. Gov. Joshua Tenorio said the declaration ensures resources would be available as the island recovers from the storm.

“We want to assure everyone, particularly areas hardest hit by Super Typhoon Champi, that all available resources will be put to use for response and recovery,” he said.

The president’s action authorizes the Department of Homeland Security’s Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate emergency assistance to save lives, protect property, and public health and safety, and lessen or avert the threat of a catastrophe.

Super Typhoon Champi made its closest approach the the Marianas about 10 miles off Guam’s southern tip around sunrise Sunday, delivering destructive winds and hazardous conditions.

The CNMI is also under a presidential emergency declaration following Gov. David Apatang’s request as Champi’s outer bands brought damaging winds and heavy seas to Saipan, Tinian and Rota. FEMA said federal assistance is available to supplement territorial and local response operations for emergency conditions beginning Oct. 16.

The declarations allow FEMA to mobilize personnel, equipment and other resources needed to address the storm’s impacts across both territories. Additional designations may be made if requested and supported by further damage assessments.

item.title: 'Good news for Guam': Champi passes 10 miles south of Malesso', moves quickly away from the island
item.description: Typhoon Champi passed just 10 miles south of Malesso’ early Sunday morning, sparing the island the full force of its 140 mph winds. Landon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said the eye of Typhoon Champi made a turn toward the west, “diving just south of the island of Guam,” and keeping the worst conditions offshore.
item.content:encoded:
Typhoon Champi passed just 10 miles south of Malesso’ early Sunday morning, sparing the island the full force of its 140 mph winds.

Landon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said the eye of Typhoon Champi made a turn toward the west, “diving just south of the island of Guam,” and keeping the worst conditions offshore.

“This is definitely good news for Guam,” he said. “This was looking very grim for us.”

The storm moved through quickly, traveling at 14 mph.

Aydlett said at the Guam International Airport, where the National Weather Service office is located, sustained winds were between 45 and 55 mph with 80 mph gusts.

“We’re going to see these conditions continue as we go through the morning hours,” Aydlett said.

Guam will continue to experience strong tropical storm-force and low-end Category 1 typhoon-force winds as the wet side of the storm passes over the island.

The front side of the storm was relatively dry, which kept rainfall totals lower than anticipated. But the backside of the system has “an abundance of showers, thunderstorms and torrential rainfall that is going to be funneling in,” he said.

Aydlett said conditions are still dangerous, and people are advised to remain indoors until winds subside.

item.title: NWS: Worst of Champi's weather will be from sunrise to late morning Sunday
item.description: Typhoon Champi was just 45 miles southeast of Guam radar at 2 a.m. Sunday, packing winds of 140 and moving to the west-northwest at 14 mph. After a night of wobbles and shifts, the Category 4 storm was forecast to pass just south of the island Sunday morning.
item.content:encoded:
Typhoon Champi was just 45 miles southeast of Guam radar at 2 a.m. Sunday, packing winds of 140 and moving to the west-northwest at 14 mph.

After a night of wobbles and shifts, the Category 4 storm was forecast to pass just south of the island Sunday morning.

At the National Weather Service Guam office, forecasters warned that the eyewall of the powerful storm could bring heavy rain and destructive winds to the island, especially to the southern villages.

Although the storm slowed down briefly, at one point dropping to a forward speed of 8 mph, Champi sped up again as it approached Guam.

Brandon Aydlett of the National Weather Service said the worst of the weather would arrive between sunrise and late morning.

“And then we’re going to see a quick reduction in those severe typhoon-force winds, but we’re still going to be seeing a lot of heavy rainfall,” he said.

High winds and heavy rain will last throughout the day and into the evening, he said.

Rainfall totals of 12-20 inches are still expected, with flooding a concern.

item.title: Pope Leo says he will gradually resume duties after cancer surgery

item.content:encoded:
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.

The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.

''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.

The pontiff said the experience of the last week "has made me feel especially close to those facing illness and infirmity." He told the faithful that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli hospital'' where he was treated.

The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.

A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing.

''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated.

"I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."

American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.

''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''

Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock.

"I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.

Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place."

"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."

Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

item.title: 'From socialite to shopgirl': American Girl Samantha gets a new story
item.description: Meet Samantha Parkington. She's a 9-year-old orphan living with her wealthy grandmother in the fictional town of Mount Bedford, N.Y., in 1904. Emily Friedrichsen, a stylist at the American Girl salon in New York City, buckles Samantha into a magenta-colored, doll-sized salon chair, affixes a pink cape around her neck, tilts her back and gets to work.
item.content:encoded:
Meet Samantha Parkington. She's a 9-year-old orphan living with her wealthy grandmother in the fictional town of Mount Bedford, N.Y., in 1904.

Emily Friedrichsen, a stylist at the American Girl salon in New York City, buckles Samantha into a magenta-colored, doll-sized salon chair, affixes a pink cape around her neck, tilts her back and gets to work.

"Before brushing your doll's hair, always make sure that you spray some water," says Amanda Holder, another stylist. "No water into the eyes, OK? And then we start brushing the hair from the bottom, the middle and then the top."

Samantha Parkington is, of course, both a children's book character and a doll — one of the most popular American Girl dolls sold in the 1990s. My Samantha doll arrived on my birthday dressed in a checked taffeta dress with a velvety pink purse, a pair of black Mary Jane shoes, a golden locket and a big bow in her shiny, brown synthetic hair.

After declaring her tangle-free, Friedrichsen turns to Samantha's bangs, which after many years of brushing, have stretched out a bit. "She can't quite see right now," Friedrichsen laughs. "So let's take care of that." Friedrichsen picks up some scissors — "Do you mind if we give her bangs a little trim? Is that OK?"

In the salon chair next to my Samantha doll is another, newer, Samantha, with her hair up in clips. Holder is using a tail comb to recurl her hair — "or you can use a crayon or a pencil" — before braiding and styling it into a twist.

The other Samantha belongs to author Fiona Davis, who was asked to write a historical fiction book for adults about Samantha Parkington to mark American Girl's 40th anniversary. It's called Samantha: The Next Chapter . "I got my doll soon after I got the job," Davis says. "She watched over my shoulder as I typed." Davis is the author of several other novels set in New York, including The Stolen Queen and The Lions of Fifth Avenue .

"In the [Samantha] book, she's 25 in 1920, and she learns that her grandmother's inheritance has been stolen," Davis says. "She basically goes from socialite to shopgirl overnight. And in her quest to find out what happened to it, it takes her to these glamorous nightclubs and to the headquarters of criminal empires."

In the café downstairs from the salon, Davis, who's 59, says that while she didn't grow up with an American Girl doll, she knew about the character from her niece.

"She explained to me that because the doll came with these stories, when you had a doll, it wasn't just playing with the doll. You became the doll," Davis says. "[My niece] talked about how she was very shy when she was a young girl and by becoming Samantha, who is a very tenacious young girl in all those stories, she was able to adopt those characteristics as well." Plus, Davis says, it made her niece a big history nerd, "which, of course, I appreciate." To write Samantha's next chapter, Davis did what she does with all her books — and dove headfirst into Samantha's history.

Pleasant Rowland launched Pleasant Company with three dolls — Samantha, Molly and Kirsten — in 1986. Her vision was a series of books and dolls "for girls about girls." It became an empire — a catalog, a magazine, a book about puberty called The Care and Keeping of You , plus stores and movies. Today, about one American Girl doll is sold every minute, according to the company.

"Pleasant Rowland is beyond brilliant," says Amanda FitzSimons, author of the new nonfiction book An American Girl: How a Billion-Dollar Doll and Its Unlikely Founder Changed Girlhood Forever . She says Rowland understood something that almost no one else in the toy industry did, "which is that girls that are between the ages of, like, 7 and 12, they want to feel important and they want to feel catered to, and there wasn't a whole lot out there that was doing that." In fact, FitzSimons says, a lot of marketers at that time were trying to make girls feel older. Rowland, she adds, "met them exactly where they were."

Each doll came with a story, which took place over six illustrated, middle-grade books. "The idea was that, you know, I'm looking at this girl and she's going through a lot of the same things I am," FitzSimons says, "and if this girl is interesting enough to write about and to learn about, then I'm interesting enough too."

Maxine Rose Schur wrote one of those original chapter books — Samantha's Surprise: A Christmas Story . "I did a lot of research in those days about Victorian Christmas — how people would decorate their homes, how they would celebrate," says Schur. She got a rough outline of the characters from Rowland but says it was up to her to add in the details.

"At that time in my life, I was watching the BBC show Upstairs, Downstairs ," Schur explains. "There's a very cranky cook — I think her name was Mrs. Bridges — I kind of fashioned the cook in Samantha's Surprise a little bit after Mrs. Bridges. So, I had a lot of fun with it."

There was also a "Look Back" or a "Peek into History" at the end of each book. Readers of Samantha's series, for example, could learn more about the suffragist movement, the role of household servants in 1904 or then-President Theodore Roosevelt's work adding land to America's national forests.

The first Pleasant Company catalog launched on Sept. 15, 1986. Two months later, FitzSimons writes in her book, the first 110,000-print run of the chapter books had sold out. Two years later, the company's annual revenue was $17 million. Part of the early success of the American Girl brand was timing — in 1987, Congress declared March Women's History Month — but Rowland was also the daughter of an advertising executive and she knew what she was doing.

"Pleasant wanted to create little toys and auxiliary materials that could be sold to complement the sale of the book and the doll," says Schur, who remembers intentionally writing ideas for accessories into Samantha's Surprise . "A certain type of little handkerchief or a little music box or other things that could be duplicated in a kind of Victorian fashion and sold."

FitzSimons says Rowland and American Girl were positioning their dolls as the anti-Barbie. "She was also marketing to parents," FitzSimons says. Nothing was pink or plastic. Samantha's table and chair set was real wicker. Her ivory tablecloth was trimmed with Battenberg lace. Her lemonade goblets — not cups — were made by a family-owned glassware company in Ohio. "The idea was really that these were things of quality for your children," FitzSimons explains. "This was an investment."

But the scope of the history covered in the American Girl books was limited, for the most part, to white, Christian, middle- to upper-class America, FitzSimons notes. In 1993, the company tried to rectify that lineup with Addy Walker, the company's first nonwhite doll, whose backstory was that she was an enslaved person who escaped to freedom in 1864.

Aisha Harris begged for an Addy doll that Christmas. "It was so cool to have this doll who kind of looked like me," she says. She remembers that Addy's hair, unlike that of a lot of the other Black dolls she played with, actually felt like her own hair. "It was kind of coarse and not as straight," Harris says.

Harris is co-host of NPR's Pop Culture Happy Hour and the author of the 2016 Slate essay " The Making of an American Girl ." She says that Addy Walker's historical background was meaningful and that she appreciated that the doll was a fully realized and researched character. Pleasant Company convened an advisory board for the doll that included Lonnie Bunch, founding director of the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.

"There's a great detail about, like, making sure that she had sort of a space between her teeth, like a gap between her teeth, because that's common for certain cultures, especially if you're coming from western Africa," Harris explains.

The problem, Harris writes in her essay, is that for nearly two decades, Addy was the only Black doll to choose from. "It's a very heavy burden to carry," she says. "Why is she the only? Why is she the only enslaved person? And why is this the only representation that I have from this company?"

Today, there are more than 50 characters in the American Girl brand, which is now owned by Mattel. They come from all different backgrounds.

According to market research company Circana , adult-only households made up 55% of toy sales in the first half of this year. Deena Taylor, senior director of global brand marketing for American Girl, says today, in addition to marketing to kids, the company is also trying to tap into that intangible, priceless quality: nostalgia. "Millennials right now, we're in that spot of, you know, wanting that familiarity of what we grew up with," Taylor says.

Millennials like me. I'm part of that generation of American Girl fans who have grown up. Who stored her doll in her mom's basement, waiting to pass her on to the next generation. Maxine Rose Schur, who wrote part of Samantha's original story, says she never previously considered what Samantha might be like as an adult. But, Schur says, "I hope she marches for women's suffrage. I think she's a feisty girl, so I don't see her as taking a back seat to a man, for example. I hope not."

No big spoilers for Samantha: The Next Chapter , but in a way, it picks up right where we left Samantha in the sixth and final book in her original series. At the end of Changes for Samantha , she attends a rally with her aunt Cornelia, a suffragist. Fifteen years later, in 1920, the 19th Amendment has just been ratified. In the very first pages of Fiona Davis' new book, we meet Samantha and her aunt discussing how they can best assist the League of Women Voters.

Davis promises that adult Samantha will be recognizable to longtime fans, but new and exciting adventures are ahead for her too. "It's fun that she's not frozen in time. She's not in amber and, you know, fossilized," Davis says. "She's out there living her life just as her readers are. And what I wanted it to be is like you were taking a long journey with an old friend but going somewhere new."

item.title: With an ad aimed at Trump, this Republican exposed GOP angst about Latino voters
item.description: MIAMI – At the heart of Little Havana neighborhood here, is Máximo Gómez Park, also known as Domino Park. Cuban Americans play games of dominos here to escape the pressures of daily life. But what started as a typical day at the park last week took a turn: Miami police arrested a player in the middle of a game after a dispute with a city worker. It spurred other players to worry about deportations
item.content:encoded:
MIAMI – At the heart of Little Havana neighborhood here, is Máximo Gómez Park, also known as Domino Park. Cuban Americans play games of dominos here to escape the pressures of daily life.

But what started as a typical day at the park last week took a turn: Miami police arrested a player in the middle of a game after a dispute with a city worker. It spurred other players to worry about deportations, setting off a broader political debate over whether President Trump or former President Biden was responsible for a higher cost of living.

"It's Biden," said Alejandro Torres, a Republican voter.

"It's Trump," responded Ricardo Carracedo, who plans to vote for Democrats in the midterm elections.

This same divide is playing out across Florida's 27th Congressional District, a Miami-Dade County seat that is more than 70% Latino. It is a warning for Republicans, whose 2024 wins relied heavily on this crucial electorate.

That year, Trump cut Democrats' margin with Latino voters nationally to just three points – down from 25 points four years earlier, according to Pew Research Center . Cuban Americans, the district's largest Latino group, have been reliable Trump supporters. But many of their friends and relatives have been swept up by the administration's deportation agenda. A crack among them could signal broader trouble for Latino support for Republican candidates.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Cuban-American Republican in her third term, has been sounding the alarm. Last month, Salazar filmed a television ad in front of the White House warning President Trump that he's "gone too far" on immigration.

"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said.

Trump hit back at Salazar after the ad. On his TruthSocial account, he shared a post in which another user called her a "back stabber."

Salazar told NPR she didn't see the comments as attacks, saying she later spoke to the president.

"I told him, 'You know, what I'm telling you is what my people are feeling,'" she said. "This is Democracy where we tell the boss, 'hey, this is what's happening in my neck of the woods.' And that's exactly what I did."

Salazar's read of the effect of Trump's policies may be right. Polling firm Equis Research found in a recent survey of registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino that if the election for Congress were held today, voters would pick the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a margin of 57 to 31.

At a Salazar campaign event this past Thursday, friends Mirla Loredo and Ramona Tunon were divided on whether they sided with her take or Trump's.

"Him, I tell you," Loredo said in Spanish.

Salazar has pushed against aggressive immigration policies in the past. For several years, she has proposed legislation she called the Dignity Act to block deportations of immigrants considered pillars of their community – such as hospitality, construction and farm workers.

Still, Carracedo, the Democratic voter from Domino Park, said he'll vote a straight blue ticket. He said Salazar's recent push against Trump's aggressive deportations is too little, too late.

"I'm not going to vote for her, because at the last hour she's defending Hispanics. But the entire time she supported Trump and the money Trump wanted for ICE," or Immigration and Customs Enforcement, he said in his native Spanish.

Trump, he said, reminds him of the communist leaders he left behind in Cuba.

In the past, Republicans' messaging on socialism had a powerful impact on this district. But now that message has lost some of its potency, eclipsed by worries about a higher cost of living and deportations.

Eduardo Gamarra, a politics professor at Florida International University, says the local economy's malaise has eclipsed all other issues.

"It's probably the number one thing. And that cuts across all of the electorate," he said.

He said the second top issue is deportations, which have devastated some Miami businesses that have lost workers and customers.

Salazar's Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, is a former broadcast journalist with Cuban roots like Salazar. He says he wants to revamp the immigration judge system, and restore federal food assistance after cuts that have hurt constituents.

Still, he concedes his party has a lot of ground to make up after largely walking away from Florida.

"One of the biggest mistakes that Democrats have made in Florida is to think that Florida is unwinnable. But I beg to differ."

Polls in the district have shifted more towards Democrats' direction in recent weeks, but Republicans are still favored. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the race "lean Republican."

Gamarra, the politics professor, says the GOP will need to rely on its political infrastructure to pull out a win

"They're not going to win on the issues ... They're going to win on turnout … the enthusiasm is on the Democrat side. But Republicans have a machinery."

item.title: Carney says 4 service members killed and dozens injured in fire at Alberta military base
item.description: Updated October 19, 2026 at 3:39 AM ChST EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on domestic soil.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 19, 2026 at 3:39 AM ChST

EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada's military on domestic soil.

Fire crews scrambled late Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation.

Speaking in a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving.

Flags would fly at half-staff on federal buildings across the country in honor of those affected by the tragedy, he said.

It was not immediately clear exactly how many people had been injured

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured. "As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family," she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (112 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster."

Acute Care Alberta said several hospitals across the province had activated a "Code Orange," an emergency designation used when multiple severely injured patients require coordinated medical care. The agency said emergency medical resources were stretched so thin that extremely few ambulances were available in the Edmonton area. It urged people to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town's small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel. He said helicopters and planes had been transporting patients to other facilities for treatment.

At least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health center late Saturday as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. One patient was seen being loaded into an ambulance.

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.

McGuinty said Sunday he was traveling to Edmonton to be briefed on the latest developments. He said the military was working closely with Alberta's government and local authorities.

The Canadian Armed Forces said it would not release casualty figures until relatives had been notified. "The full extent of the impact remains under assessment," the military said in a statement late Saturday.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.

McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.

"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said.

"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he added.

He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. "This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation."

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.
